y-m-19-01.title: Which is greater, −5/6 or −7/9? Checking a solution
y-m-19-01.goal: Use the number line to see that for negative fractions with the same denominator, a larger numerator means a smaller number, then find the line in the solution that goes wrong and fix it.
y-m-19-01.material: Jihu and Seoyun solved a problem comparing −5/6 and −7/9 to see which is greater. (−5/6 is read 'negative five sixths' and −7/9 is read 'negative seven ninths'. On a number line, the number farther to the right is greater.) Below is Jihu's solution.
y-m-19-01.thinking.0: Find the first line where the solution goes wrong
y-m-19-01.thinking.1: Check the conclusion using other representations (decimals, number line)
y-m-19-01.thinking.2: Explain in words the direction of size comparison for negative numbers
y-m-19-01.prereq.0: The number farther to the right on a number line is greater
y-m-19-01.s.s1.prompt: Choose the first line in Jihu's solution where the thinking goes wrong.
y-m-19-01.s.s1.hint.1: Place the result of each line on the number line, one at a time, and check whether that line is also correct on the number line.
y-m-19-01.s.s1.line.0: Make the two denominators the same. The least common multiple of 6 and 9 is 18.
y-m-19-01.s.s1.line.2: The denominators are the same, so compare only the numerators. Since 15 > 14, −15/18 > −14/18.
y-m-19-01.s.s1.line.3: So −5/6 is the greater number than −7/9.
y-m-19-01.s.s1.explain: It goes wrong at line 3. It is true that the numerator 15 is greater than 14, but with a minus sign in front, −15/18 is to the left of −14/18 on the number line. So −14/18 is the greater number, and the conclusion in line 4 changes to −7/9 being greater.
y-m-19-01.s.s2.prompt: After fixing the line, you want to check once more that the conclusion is right. What is the most reliable way to check?
y-m-19-01.s.s2.hint.0: For each option, ask yourself: 'Can this method tell me which of the two numbers is farther to the right?'
y-m-19-01.s.s2.hint.1: Actually apply each option to −5/6 and −7/9 and try it yourself to see whether a conclusion comes out.
y-m-19-01.s.s2.explain: If you change the fractions to decimals and place them on the number line, −0.83… is to the left of −0.77…. Checking means seeing whether a different route from the first solution gives the same conclusion (−7/9 is greater).
y-m-19-01.s.s3.prompt: Tell Jihu how to fix line 3. Write two or three sentences that include how the size of the numerator and the size of the number are related when the number is negative.
y-m-19-01.s.s3.hint.0: First, say which of −15/18 and −14/18 is farther from 0.
y-m-19-01.s.s3.hint.1: Start by completing a sentence with a blank, like 'For negative numbers, the more ○○, the smaller the number.'
y-m-19-01.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you check that the direction of the inequality sign you fixed matches the positions on the number line?
y-m-19-01.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did your explanation include why the rule 'a bigger numerator means a bigger number' is true only for positive numbers?
y-m-19-01.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you write the fixed line specifically enough that Jihu can follow it and solve the problem?
y-m-19-01.s.s3.model.0: A negative number is smaller the farther it is from 0. 15/18 is farther from 0 than 14/18, so −15/18 is farther to the left, that is, smaller. So line 3 should be fixed to −15/18 < −14/18.
y-m-19-01.s.s3.model.1: If you place −15 and −14 on the number line, −14 is on the right. For negative numbers, the size of the numerator and the size of the number go in opposite directions, so the direction of the inequality sign in line 3 must be written the other way around.
y-m-19-01.s.s3.modelNote.1: An explanation based on position on the number line
y-m-19-01.prereq.1: Writing fractions with the same denominator by finding a common denominator (learned in elementary school)
y-m-19-01.prereq.2: Negative numbers and the number line (at the level of the Integers and Rational Numbers unit in middle school grade 1)
y-m-19-01.s.s1.hint.0: Check in order from the top whether each line follows correctly from the line right before it.
y-m-19-01.s.s2.o.a: Make and apply one more rule that the bigger the denominator, the smaller the number
y-m-19-01.s.s2.r.a: With negative numbers, the size order is not decided by the size of the denominator or numerator alone. Rather than adding rules, you should go back and check using position on the number line.
y-m-19-01.s.s2.o.b: Plot the decimals −0.83… and −0.77… on the number line and find the number further to the right
y-m-19-01.s.s2.r.b: This is a method of changing to a different form and checking again by the same standard (position on the number line). You can check whether the conclusion is the same even if the solving method differs.
y-m-19-01.s.s2.o.c: Place 5/6 and 7/9, the two fractions multiplied by −1, on the number line and use the inequality sign in the same direction as it is
y-m-19-01.s.s2.r.c: Multiplying by −1 reverses the order of sizes. If you use the same direction, the same kind of error as Jihu's happens again.
y-m-19-01.s.s2.o.d: Find the sum of the two numbers on the number line and check whether it is negative
y-m-19-01.s.s2.r.d: That the sum is negative only tells you that both are negative. It does not tell you which one is bigger.
y-m-19-01.s.s3.model.2: On the number line, −15 is to the left of −14. If the numerator is bigger, it is actually a smaller number, so line 3 is −15/18<−14/18.
y-m-19-01.s.s3.model.3: On the number line, −15/18 is further from 0 than −14/18 and is to the left, so it is smaller. For negative numbers, the one with the larger absolute value is the smaller number.

y-m-19-02.title: How can we trust the value of (−1)×(−2)?
y-m-19-02.topic: Multiplying negative numbers and the reasons behind the rule
y-m-19-02.goal: Tell apart how different kinds of evidence (a pattern, the distributive law, a real-life interpretation) support the conclusion (negative)×(negative)=positive, and adjust how confident you are as more information arrives.
y-m-19-02.material: Suppose you already know (positive)×(negative) in integer multiplication. (−2) is read 'negative two', and (−1)×(−2) is read 'negative one times negative two'. Let's see how your thinking about the value of (−1)×(−2) changes as information is given one piece at a time.
y-m-19-02.thinking.0: Predict the next value from a pattern
y-m-19-02.thinking.1: Check how new information changes your confidence
y-m-19-02.thinking.2: Tell apart evidence, reasons, and analogies
y-m-19-02.prereq.0: Multiplying a positive and a negative number (e.g., 3×(−2)=−6)
y-m-19-02.prereq.1: Experience calculating a product with a sum in parentheses (distributive law) using natural numbers
y-m-19-02.s.s1.prompt: The information is revealed one piece at a time. Each time, pick what seems most likely to you right now, then check your thinking against the information that follows.
y-m-19-02.s.s1.hint.0: For each piece of information, tell apart whether what you newly learned 'makes your expectation firmer' or 'makes you think about the range of your expectation'.
y-m-19-02.s.s1.hint.1: Put the answer you chose directly into the expression and check that it does not contradict the earlier information.
y-m-19-02.s.s1.st.0.info:
I wrote down the values multiplied by (−2) while lowering the multiplier through 3, 2, 1, 0.
3 × (−2) = −6
2 × (−2) = −4
1 × (−2) = −2
0 × (−2) = 0
y-m-19-02.s.s1.st.0.ask: Look at how the result changes each time the multiplier in the table goes down by 1, and predict the value of the next line, (−1) × (−2).
y-m-19-02.s.s1.st.0.after: Continuing the pattern and predicting 2 is reasonable, and so is wanting to check more because there is no guarantee that the pattern continues. A pattern is only evidence, not a proof.
y-m-19-02.s.s1.st.0.o.a: 2. The result has been getting bigger by 2 each time, so the next one will be 2 too
y-m-19-02.s.s1.st.0.r.a: This is a prediction made by continuing the table's pattern to the next cell. It assumes that the pattern keeps going.
y-m-19-02.s.s1.st.0.o.b: −2. We are multiplying by a negative number, so the result will be negative too
y-m-19-02.s.s1.st.0.r.b: This only uses a sense of signs: 'a negative number is involved, so the answer is negative'. It does not yet use how the results in the table are changing.
y-m-19-02.s.s1.st.0.o.c: I don't know yet. I need to check separately whether this pattern continues into the negative cells
y-m-19-02.s.s1.st.0.r.c: This is the attitude of using the pattern as evidence while considering its range. A pattern does not guarantee that it continues.
y-m-19-02.s.s1.st.0.r.d: This assumes that 0 is 'the end'. The table gives no reason to stop at 0.
y-m-19-02.s.s1.st.1.info:
New information: Suppose the distributive law you used with natural numbers (multiplying a sum in parentheses is the same as multiplying each part and adding) keeps holding for negative numbers too. Then
(−1) × (−2) + 1 × (−2) = ((−1) + 1) × (−2) = 0 × (−2) = 0
and 1 × (−2) = −2.
y-m-19-02.s.s1.st.1.ask: After seeing this information, how did your thinking about (−1) × (−2) change?
y-m-19-02.s.s1.st.1.after: It is reasonable to keep your first prediction (2) and become more confident, and it is also reasonable to point out that this conclusion depends on the promise that 'the distributive law keeps holding'.
y-m-19-02.s.s1.st.1.o.a: 0. The result of the expression above is 0, so the value of (−1)×(−2) must be 0 too
y-m-19-02.s.s1.st.1.r.a: This treats the value 0 of the whole expression as the same as the value of one term inside it. That one term is the number that gives 0 when added to −2.
y-m-19-02.s.s1.st.1.o.b: Change it to −2. If the two terms are both −2, the expression looks tidy and neat
y-m-19-02.s.s1.st.1.r.b: (−2)+(−2)=−4, so the sum is not 0. The step of putting it into the expression to check is missing.
y-m-19-02.s.s1.st.1.o.c: It is decided to be 2 under the promise that the distributive law keeps holding. If the promise changes, it could be different
y-m-19-02.s.s1.st.1.r.c: This even looks at what assumption the conclusion depends on. It is a judgment that is aware of the range where a rule applies.
y-m-19-02.s.s1.st.1.o.d: I'm more sure of 2. To add up to 0 with −2, it has to be the opposite of −2
y-m-19-02.s.s1.st.1.r.d: The new information made your first prediction firmer. You decided the value using the condition that it is the number that gives 0 when added.
y-m-19-02.s.s1.st.2.info: New information: Jaemin said, "I don't know what it means to have a debt of 2원 −1 times. If it can't be explained in real life, I can't believe (−1)×(−2)=2." On the other hand, this multiplication can also be interpreted as '−2 is 2 to the left, and multiplying by −1 flips the direction'.
y-m-19-02.s.s1.st.2.ask: What do you think about Jaemin's opinion?
y-m-19-02.s.s1.st.2.after: It is reasonable to not reject a rule just because there is no real-life example, and to separate the roles of the consistency of the rule and of interpretation.
y-m-19-02.s.s1.st.2.o.a: Not having an explanation in real life does not make it wrong. I check whether it conflicts with the other rules
y-m-19-02.s.s1.st.2.r.a: You found the reason for accepting the conclusion not in a single real-life example but in the consistency of the whole set of rules.
y-m-19-02.s.s1.st.2.o.b: There is a rule and an interpretation (flipping direction), so I accept it, but I remember that the interpretation is only an analogy
y-m-19-02.s.s1.st.2.r.b: You separated the roles of a rule and an analogy. You see an interpretation as a help, not the whole basis.
y-m-19-02.s.s1.st.2.o.c: If there is even one way to interpret it in real life, this result has been fully proved
y-m-19-02.s.s1.st.2.r.c: An interpretation helps understanding, but one interpretation is not a proof. You also separately need it not to conflict with the rules.
y-m-19-02.s.s1.st.2.o.d: A rule that cannot be explained right away with real-life examples must be considered a wrong rule
y-m-19-02.s.s1.st.2.r.d: Not every rule in math can be explained right away with real-life examples. A rule is not wrong just because there is no way to explain it.
y-m-19-02.s.s1.reflect: The pattern was evidence that 'it seems to continue', the distributive law was a reason that 'if we keep the promise, it is decided this way', and the real-life interpretation was an 'analogy that helps understanding'. Look back at how your confidence in the same conclusion changed each time the kind of basis changed.
y-m-19-02.s.s2.prompt: You want to explain to a friend that (−3) × (−2) = 6. Choose everything that can be used as a reason.
y-m-19-02.s.s2.hint.0: For each option, ask one more time 'Then why is that?' and check whether the answer keeps going.
y-m-19-02.s.s2.hint.1: Try using each option's explanation as it is on other cases like (−3)×(−3) or (−2)×(−2) and test whether it works.
y-m-19-02.s.s2.r.a: This decided the value using only the distributive law and multiplication you already know. It is a reason drawn from earlier rules without any new promise.
y-m-19-02.s.s2.o.b: I put it into a calculator and the value 6 came out, and it was the same no matter how many times I pressed, so the expression is right
y-m-19-02.s.s2.r.b: A calculator is also built on the same rules. It only shows the result and does not explain why.
y-m-19-02.s.s2.o.c: When there are two minus signs they cancel each other out, so the product becomes positive, and that is the reason
y-m-19-02.s.s2.r.c: It is an easy-to-remember analogy, but not a reason. It cannot explain what happens with three minus signs.
y-m-19-02.s.s2.o.d: If you lower the multiplier through 3, 2, 1, …, the result gets bigger by 2 each time, and this pattern continues to (−3)×(−2)
y-m-19-02.s.s2.r.d: This is evidence from continuing the table's pattern into the negative cells. It is not a proof, but it is supporting evidence.
y-m-19-02.s.s2.explain: Continuing the pattern in the table and deciding the value with the distributive law both support the value 6. The calculator result and the 'cancelling out' analogy do not explain the reason.

y-m-19-03.title: Drawing three cards whose product is 20 or more
y-m-19-03.topic: Multiplying integers and the sign of a product
y-m-19-03.goal: Use the relationship between the number of negative cards and the sign of the product to find several combinations that meet the condition, and decide how to avoid missing the greatest product.
y-m-19-03.material: There are five cards. The numbers on the cards are −6, −4, −1, 2, 5. (−6 is read 'negative six'.) Draw three different cards and multiply the three numbers. The cards must be all different cards, taken one at a time.
y-m-19-03.thinking.0: Narrow down the candidates using the sign condition
y-m-19-03.thinking.1: Make several solutions that meet the condition
y-m-19-03.thinking.2: Decide how to find the greatest value without missing any
y-m-19-03.prereq.0: Multiplying integers (a negative times a negative, a product of three numbers)
y-m-19-03.s.s1.prompt: When you draw three of these five cards, the product is positive when how many of the drawn cards are negative?
y-m-19-03.s.s1.hint.0: Multiply out the cases of drawing 1, 2, and 3 negative cards one at a time and check just the signs first.
y-m-19-03.s.s1.hint.1: Count how many times a negative sign appeared in the multiplication.
y-m-19-03.s.s1.r.a: There are only two positive cards, 2 and 5. You can't draw three cards without a negative one, so this case can't happen with these cards.
y-m-19-03.s.s1.r.b: The product of 1 negative card and 2 positive cards has one negative number multiplied in, so it is negative.
y-m-19-03.s.s1.r.c: The product of two negative cards becomes positive first, and multiplying by the remaining positive card keeps it positive.
y-m-19-03.s.s1.r.d: Multiplying three negative cards means a negative number was multiplied three times, so the result is negative again.
y-m-19-03.s.s1.explain: If the number of negative cards in the product is even, the product is positive; if it is odd, the product is negative. With these cards, it is only possible when 2 of the 3 cards are negative (with 0 cards there are not enough positive cards).
y-m-19-03.s.s2.prompt: Make three combinations of three different cards whose product is 20 or more. Write the numbers on the cards in a, b, c, from smallest to largest.
y-m-19-03.s.s2.hint.0: First, try pairing two negative cards with one positive card.
y-m-19-03.s.s2.hint.1: If the product comes out smaller than 20, keep the same two negative cards and swap in a different positive card.
y-m-19-03.s.s2.var.a: The number on the smallest card
y-m-19-03.s.s2.var.b: The number on the middle card
y-m-19-03.s.s2.var.c: The number on the largest card
y-m-19-03.s.s2.ok.c1: All three numbers are numbers on the cards.
y-m-19-03.s.s2.fail.c1: Some number is not on the cards. Choose from −6, −4, −1, 2, 5.
y-m-19-03.s.s2.ok.c2: They are three different cards, written from the smallest number.
y-m-19-03.s.s2.fail.c2: Write them in order from the smallest number, using different cards.
y-m-19-03.s.s2.fail.c3: The product is less than 20. Check the sign of the product first.
y-m-19-03.s.s2.explain: The possible combinations are (−6, −4, 5)=120, (−6, −4, 2)=48, (−6, −1, 5)=30, (−4, −1, 5)=20. All of them have 2 negative cards.
y-m-19-03.s.s3.prompt: What is the most reliable way to be sure that you found the combination with the greatest product without missing any?
y-m-19-03.s.s3.hint.0: First filter the candidate cases that meet the condition by sign.
y-m-19-03.s.s3.hint.1: Count how many candidates remain after filtering and write the products of all of them in a table.
y-m-19-03.s.s3.o.a: Draw the three cards with the biggest numbers, 5, 2, −1, and multiply them
y-m-19-03.s.s3.r.a: Bigger numbers do not mean a bigger product. If even one negative number is mixed in, the product becomes negative.
y-m-19-03.s.s3.o.b: If the product of the first combination you found is over 20, it is the greatest
y-m-19-03.s.s3.r.b: Going over the condition '20 or more' and being the greatest are different things. Another combination could be greater.
y-m-19-03.s.s3.o.c: Draw −6, −4, −1. Multiplying the digits gives 24, so it will be the greatest
y-m-19-03.s.s3.r.c: You left out the sign. The product of three negative cards is −24, so it is actually smaller.
y-m-19-03.s.s3.o.d: Find all the combinations with a positive product (2 negative cards + 1 positive card) and compare them
y-m-19-03.s.s3.r.d: This method first narrows the candidates by sign and then compares the remaining candidates without missing any. It gives you a reason to believe that no combination was missed.
y-m-19-03.s.s3.explain: The combinations with a positive product are the 6 ways of choosing 2 of the 3 negative cards and 1 of the 2 positive cards. The products are 48, 120, 12, 30, 8, 20, and comparing all of them lets you be sure that the greatest product 120 is (−6, −4, 5).

y-m-19-04.title: Finding a number to multiply 72 by to get the square of some number
y-m-19-04.topic: Multiplying to make a square number (number of prime factors)
y-m-19-04.goal: Find not just one but several numbers that make a square number when multiplied, and explain in words the rule they all share.
y-m-19-04.thinking.0: Make several solutions that meet the constraints
y-m-19-04.thinking.1: Find the common rule among several solutions
y-m-19-04.thinking.2: Explain the relationship between the smallest solution and the others
y-m-19-04.prereq.0: The meaning of a square number (e.g., 36=6×6)
y-m-19-04.prereq.2: Writing a number as a product (e.g., 72=8×9)
y-m-19-04.s.s1.prompt: What is the smallest natural number a that makes a square number when multiplied by 72?
y-m-19-04.s.s1.hint.0: Write down the square numbers near 72, 64 and 81, and check whether 72 is a square number.
y-m-19-04.s.s1.hint.1: Write 72 as the product of two numbers, 8×9, and look at which of them is already the square of some number.
y-m-19-04.s.s1.r.a: First you need to check whether 72 itself is a square number. 72 is between 8×8=64 and 9×9=81, so it is not a square number.
y-m-19-04.s.s1.r.b: In 72=2×2×2×3×3, the 3s are paired up, and one 2 is left over. If you multiply by one more 2, it has the form where everything is paired.
y-m-19-04.s.s1.r.c: 72×3=216. It is between 14×14=196 and 15×15=225, so it is not a square number. Multiplying by 3 makes three 3s, which actually breaks the pairing.
y-m-19-04.s.s1.r.d: 72×8=576=24×24, so it is true that it becomes a square number. But you did not check whether any smaller number also works.
y-m-19-04.s.s1.explain: If you write 72 as 2×2×2×3×3, the 3s are paired and one 2 is left over. Multiplying by 2 gives 2×2×2×2×3×3 = (2×2×3)×(2×2×3) = 12×12. 1 doesn't work, so the smallest number is 2.
y-m-19-04.s.s2.prompt: Find three different numbers a that make a square number when multiplied by 72. (Natural numbers from 1 to 100)
y-m-19-04.s.s2.hint.0: Start from the smallest number, 2, and test whether multiplying 2 by some number keeps giving square numbers.
y-m-19-04.s.s2.hint.1: Write each product you made as a product of the same two numbers to check it.
y-m-19-04.s.s2.var.a: The number a to multiply 72 by
y-m-19-04.s.s2.fail.c1: a is a number from 1 to 100.
y-m-19-04.s.s2.fail.c2: Write a as a natural number.
y-m-19-04.s.s2.ok.c3: The value multiplied with 72 is a square number.
y-m-19-04.s.s2.fail.c3: The value multiplied with 72 is not the square of any natural number. Find the product and check whether it can be written as a product of two equal numbers.
y-m-19-04.s.s2.explain: 2, 8, 18, 32, 50, 72, 98 all work. For example, 72×18 = 1296 = 36×36. There are seven in all that are 100 or less.
y-m-19-04.s.s3.hint.0: Write each a you found as 2×(some number) and put the numbers in parentheses side by side.
y-m-19-04.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you check whether the rule you wrote also works for the a you haven't found yet (e.g., 72, 98)?
y-m-19-04.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you explain 'why 2 must be included' by connecting it to the way 72 is written as a product?
y-m-19-04.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Can you also predict the next number from your rule that goes over 100?
y-m-19-04.s.s3.model.0: a is 2, 8, 18, 32, 50, and all of them are 2 times a square number such as 1, 4, 9, 16, 25. So when multiplied with 72, one more 2 appears, the factors pair up, and it becomes a square number.
y-m-19-04.s.s3.model.1: 72 is a number made by multiplying 2 three times and 3 twice. One 2 is left over, so a has to include one more 2, and then you can multiply by any number twice. So you get 2, 2×2×2=8, 2×3×3=18.
y-m-19-04.s.s3.modelNote.1: An explanation using pairs in the multiplication
y-m-19-04.material: We want to multiply 72 by a natural number a so that the product becomes the square of some natural number (a number made by multiplying the same number twice). For example, it is like multiplying 12 by 3 to get 12×3 = 36 = 6×6. Only think of a as a natural number from 1 to 100.
y-m-19-04.s.s3.prompt: If you line up the a's you found from smallest, what common pattern do you see? Write the rule in your own words.
y-m-19-04.s.s3.hint.1: Line up the numbers that appeared in the parentheses from smallest, and write each number as a multiplication.
y-m-19-04.s.s3.model.2: The a's I found are 2 multiplied by 1, 4, 9, 16.

y-m-19-05.title: Are there no fractions at all between 1/3 and 1/2?
y-m-19-05.topic: Sizes of rational numbers and numbers between two numbers
y-m-19-05.goal: Test a claim with examples, make several fractions between two fractions, and understand that there are endlessly many such numbers.
y-m-19-05.material: Mina said, "There is no fraction at all between 1/3 and 1/2. Both numerators are 1, and the denominators 3 and 2 are next to each other." (1/3 is read 'one third'.) Think only about fractions whose denominator and numerator are both natural numbers.
y-m-19-05.thinking.1: Make several fractions that meet the condition
y-m-19-05.thinking.2: Decide whether intuition from experience (integers) can be used for fractions as it is
y-m-19-05.prereq.0: Comparing the sizes of fractions (Grade 5 elementary level)
y-m-19-05.prereq.2: A rational number is a number that can be written as a fraction
y-m-19-05.s.s1.prompt: You want to check whether Mina's statement is right. What would be good to do first?
y-m-19-05.s.s1.hint.0: Change 1/3 and 1/2 to decimals and think of one number between 0.33… and 0.5.
y-m-19-05.s.s1.hint.1: Write the number you thought of as a fraction and check whether it is greater than 1/3 and less than 1/2.
y-m-19-05.s.s1.o.a: Accept that since there is no integer between neighboring integers, the same must be true for fractions
y-m-19-05.s.s1.r.a: You carried over an experience that was true for integers to fractions as it is. You need to test separately whether it is also true for fractions.
y-m-19-05.s.s1.o.b: Change the denominator to 6, look at 2/6 and 3/6, and if there is no fraction between them, conclude from that
y-m-19-05.s.s1.r.b: You tested only one denominator, 6. If you choose a different denominator, the result could be different.
y-m-19-05.s.s1.o.c: Collect only fractions with numerator 1 and look for a denominator between 3 and 2
y-m-19-05.s.s1.r.c: If the denominator is a natural number, there is no natural number between 3 and 2. Restricting the numerator to 1 narrowed the problem down.

y-m-19-05.s.s1.r.d: The statement 'there is none at all' is broken by one example. This is the most direct way to test a claim.
y-m-19-05.s.s1.explain: The claim 'there is none at all' is broken by finding just one fraction in between. Looking for one first is the most direct test.
y-m-19-05.s.s2.prompt: Make three fractions p/q with different values that are greater than 1/3 and less than 1/2. (The numerator p and denominator q are natural numbers, and the denominator is 40 or less.)
y-m-19-05.s.s2.hint.0: Change the denominator to 5, 7, 8, 9, and so on, choose a numerator for each, and check the decimal value.
y-m-19-05.s.s2.hint.1: Be careful that fractions with the same value (e.g., 2/5 and 4/10) are counted as one.

y-m-19-05.s.s2.fail.c1: Write a numerator of 1 or more and a denominator from 2 to 40.

y-m-19-05.s.s2.fail.c4: It is not less than 1/2. Change it to a decimal and compare it with 0.5.
y-m-19-05.s.s2.explain: 2/5=0.4, 3/8=0.375, 5/12=0.41666…, 3/7=0.428…, 4/9=0.444… are all between 0.333… and 0.5. Even with denominators of 40 or less, there are several. A fraction with the same value, like 4/10, is counted as one.
y-m-19-05.s.s3.prompt: Then how many fractions are there in total between 1/3 and 1/2?
y-m-19-05.s.s3.hint.0: Double the denominator each time to 6, 12, 24, rewrite 1/3 and 1/2, and compare how many numerators lie between the two fractions.
y-m-19-05.s.s3.hint.1: Predict what happens to the numerators that can fit in between if you make the denominator bigger once more.

y-m-19-05.s.s3.r.a: You pointed out that each time the denominator gets bigger, the gaps between numerators increase, so new fractions can keep being made.
y-m-19-05.s.s3.o.b: None at all. If you make the denominator 6, 2/6 and 3/6 are right next to each other
y-m-19-05.s.s3.r.b: If you make the denominator 6, the numerators look like they are next to each other, but if you make the denominator bigger, to 12, 24, …, new numerators appear in between.
y-m-19-05.s.s3.o.c: If you limit the denominator to 40 or less, the count is fixed, so that is all there is
y-m-19-05.s.s3.r.c: You counted with an upper limit on the denominator, not all fractions. If you go past the limit, you can find more.
y-m-19-05.s.s3.o.d: Exactly one, only 5/12 in the exact middle of the two fractions
y-m-19-05.s.s3.r.d: 5/12 is only one of the fractions in between. We already found 3/7 and 4/9 too, so it is not just one.
y-m-19-05.s.s3.explain: If you make the denominator bigger, the numerators fit more closely in the same interval. For example, with denominator 12, 5/12 lies between 1/3=4/12 and 1/2=6/12, and if you make the denominator 24, there are 9/24, 10/24, 11/24. You can say there is no end.

y-m-19-06.title: When the temperature differs by 7℃, what else do we need to know?
y-m-19-06.topic: Adding and subtracting integers (the meaning of a difference)
y-m-19-06.goal: Confirm that the information 'the difference is 7' alone does not determine a single value, and decide what more information is needed to determine one.
y-m-19-06.material: One day, the temperature at 9 a.m. was −3℃ (3 degrees below zero). They say the temperature at 3 p.m. differed from the 9 a.m. temperature by 7℃. All temperatures are given as integers (℃). Let the 3 p.m. temperature be t℃, and the difference is the larger of the two temperatures minus the smaller.
y-m-19-06.thinking.0: Find all the values that meet the condition
y-m-19-06.thinking.1: Decide whether the information is enough
y-m-19-06.thinking.2: State specifically what extra information is needed
y-m-19-06.prereq.1: The distance between two numbers on a number line
y-m-19-06.s.s1.prompt: Find two different values of the 3 p.m. temperature t that differ from the 9 a.m. temperature by 7℃.
y-m-19-06.s.s1.hint.0: Mark −3 on a number line and count how many places are 7 steps away from it.
y-m-19-06.s.s1.hint.1: Calculate directly the difference (larger minus smaller) between the value you found and −3.
y-m-19-06.s.s1.fail.c1: Write the temperature as an integer.
y-m-19-06.s.s1.fail.c2: The difference from −3℃ is not 7℃. Check the places 7 steps away from −3 on the number line.
y-m-19-06.s.s1.explain: 7 steps to the right from −3 is 4℃, and 7 steps to the left is −10℃. Both values differ by 7℃.
y-m-19-06.s.s2.prompt: What more would you need to know to decide the 3 p.m. temperature as one value? Choose everything that, if you knew just that one thing, would decide it.
y-m-19-06.s.s2.hint.1: For each option, check: 'If I know this information, can I tell 4 and −10 apart?'
y-m-19-06.s.s2.o.a: The exact number of hours that passed between the two times
y-m-19-06.s.s2.r.a: How much time passed does not tell you whether the temperature went up or down.
y-m-19-06.s.s2.o.b: Whether 3 p.m. was warmer or colder than 9 a.m.
y-m-19-06.s.s2.r.b: This is information that decides whether to go right or left from −3. It settles on one of the two.
y-m-19-06.s.s2.o.c: Whether the 3 p.m. temperature is above or below 0℃ (zero degrees)
y-m-19-06.s.s2.r.c: 4℃ is above 0℃ and −10℃ is below, so this information also tells the two apart.
y-m-19-06.s.s2.o.d: A value re-checked to confirm that the 9 a.m. temperature really was −3℃
y-m-19-06.s.s2.r.d: Whether the given value is right has nothing to do with the cause of the value splitting into two in this problem.
y-m-19-06.s.s2.explain: If you know 'it was warmer' or 'it is above 0℃', it is decided to be either 4℃ or −10℃. How many hours passed, or whether the value already given is right, does not help.
y-m-19-06.s.s3.prompt: A friend declared, "The temperature at 3 p.m. is 4℃." Explain to your friend why the information is still not enough, together with which values are possible.
y-m-19-06.s.s3.hint.0: First write two possible afternoon temperatures, and then write in one sentence why those two are different.
y-m-19-06.s.s3.hint.1: In the last sentence, put 'If you know ○○, it is decided as one'.
y-m-19-06.s.s3.placeholder: Example: The afternoon temperature could be ... or ... Because ...
y-m-19-06.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you say, using an expression or a number line, how you found each of the two possible values?
y-m-19-06.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you write specifically 'what extra information would make it one value'?
y-m-19-06.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you avoid insisting your friend's answer 4℃ is wrong, and admit that it could be so?
y-m-19-06.s.s3.model.0: The afternoon temperature could be 4℃, which is 7 higher than −3, or −10℃, which is 7 lower. You need to know whether the afternoon was warmer or colder than the morning to decide on one.
y-m-19-06.s.s3.model.1: The statement that the difference is 7 holds whether it went up or down, so 4℃ or −10℃ are possible. To say it is 4℃, you need to know that the afternoon temperature was above 0℃.
y-m-19-06.s.s3.modelNote.1: An explanation that gives whether it is above or below 0℃ as the extra information
y-m-19-06.s.s2.hint.0: Think about what information would tell you which of the two values found in the previous step it is.
y-m-19-06.s.s3.model.2: Both 4 and −10 are possible. If you know whether it was warmer or colder than the morning, it can be decided.
y-m-19-06.s.s3.model.3: It could be 4 or -10. You need to know whether it went up or down.

y-m-19-07.title: Comparing ways to find the midpoint of two numbers on a number line
y-m-19-07.topic: Two numbers on a number line and the number exactly in the middle
y-m-19-07.goal: Compare different ways of finding the midpoint to sort out correct methods from misconceptions, and make several pairs of numbers that have the same midpoint.
y-m-19-07.material: On a number line, point A is at −7 (negative seven) and point B is at 5. Four people described different ways to find the position of point M, the midpoint of A and B. (The distance between A and B is 5−(−7)=12.)
y-m-19-07.thinking.0: Compare methods and find the errors
y-m-19-07.thinking.1: Make several pairs that meet the condition
y-m-19-07.thinking.2: Test whether the method also works with decimals
y-m-19-07.prereq.0: The positions of integers on a number line
y-m-19-07.prereq.1: Adding integers, the distance between two numbers (larger number − smaller number)
y-m-19-07.s.s1.prompt: Choose all the methods that find the position of M correctly.
y-m-19-07.s.s1.hint.0: Mark −7 and 5 on a number line, and measure whether the distance from the point you think is the midpoint to A and to B is the same.
y-m-19-07.s.s1.hint.1: First tell apart whether the value each method finds is a 'position' or a 'distance'.
y-m-19-07.s.s1.o.a: Seohyeon: To find the position, add the absolute values 7 and 5 of −7 and 5 and divide by 2, which gives 6.
y-m-19-07.s.s1.r.a: The absolute value is the distance from 0, so removing the signs changes the position. 6 is not the midpoint of A and B.
y-m-19-07.s.s1.o.b: Jisu: Add the two numbers and divide by 2. (−7+5)÷2 = −1
y-m-19-07.s.s1.r.b: This used the idea that the average of the two numbers is the midpoint. The key is that the signs were kept when adding.
y-m-19-07.s.s1.o.c: Doyun: Divide the distance 12 between A and B in half, and 6 is the position of M.
y-m-19-07.s.s1.r.c: 6 is the distance from A to M. To get a position, you have to move that far from the starting point.
y-m-19-07.s.s1.o.d: Hayun: Move half of the distance 12, which is 6, to the right from A. −7+6 = −1
y-m-19-07.s.s1.r.d: After halving the distance, you moved from the starting point to get a position. A different route gives the same position.
y-m-19-07.s.s1.explain: (−7+5)÷2 = −1, and going half the distance, 6, to the right from A also gives −7+6 = −1. 6 is just the distance, or the average of the absolute values, and not the position of M.
y-m-19-07.s.s2.prompt: Make three different pairs (a, b) of integers whose midpoint is −1 (negative one) and whose distance apart is 4 or more. (Write a as the smaller number than b.)
y-m-19-07.s.s2.hint.0: Go some steps to the left of −1 and the same number of steps to the right.
y-m-19-07.s.s2.hint.1: Change the number of steps to 1, 2, 3, … and write them in a table, then pick only the rows where the distance is 4 or more.
y-m-19-07.s.s2.var.a: The number a of the left point
y-m-19-07.s.s2.var.b: The number b of the right point
y-m-19-07.s.s2.ok.c1: They are integers and a is less than b.
y-m-19-07.s.s2.fail.c1: a and b must be integers, and a must be less than b.
y-m-19-07.s.s2.fail.c2: The midpoint is not −1. Calculate the midpoint of the two numbers to check.
y-m-19-07.s.s2.ok.c3: The distance between the two points is 4 or more.
y-m-19-07.s.s2.fail.c3: The distance between the two points is less than 4.
y-m-19-07.s.s2.explain: If the midpoint is −1, then a and b are on opposite sides of −1 at the same distance: (−3, 1), (−4, 2), (−5, 3), (−6, 4), (−7, 5), … If the distance must be 4 or more, it starts from (−3, 1).
y-m-19-07.s.s3.prompt: What is the midpoint of −2.5 (negative two point five) and 4? Find it using one of the methods you counted as correct above, and write why that method also works for numbers that are not integers.
y-m-19-07.s.s3.hint.0: First roughly mark −2.5 and 4 on a number line, and predict whether the midpoint will be to the right or left of 0.
y-m-19-07.s.s3.hint.1: Measure the distance from the value you found with the method above to each of the two points, and check whether they are equal.
y-m-19-07.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you check that the value found with your method is the same distance from −2.5 and from 4?
y-m-19-07.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you explain why it works for decimals, for example, 'distances on a number line are measured the same way even for decimals'?
y-m-19-07.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you check once more whether another method gives the same value?
y-m-19-07.s.s3.model.0: (−2.5+4)÷2 = 1.5÷2 = 0.75. Adding two numbers and dividing by 2 can be done in the same way even if the numbers are decimals, and the distances from 0.75 to −2.5 and to 4 are both equally 3.25.
y-m-19-07.s.s3.model.1: The distance is 4−(−2.5)=6.5 and half of it is 3.25. Going 3.25 to the right from −2.5 gives 0.75. Distances on a number line are measured in the same way as with integers.
y-m-19-07.s.s3.modelNote.1: The method of moving half the distance from the starting point

y-m-19-08.title: Testing the claim 'division is also the same if you swap the order'
y-m-19-08.topic: Dividing integers and the commutative law
y-m-19-08.goal: Test with examples whether a property that is true for multiplication can be applied to division as it is, and state the condition for when it holds.
y-m-19-08.material: Minjae said, "Like 2×3 = 3×2, multiplication gives the same value even if you swap the order. So division should be the same if you swap the order too. a÷b = b÷a." Here a and b are nonzero integers. ('a÷b' is read 'a divided by b'.)
y-m-19-08.thinking.1: Find the condition for when it holds
y-m-19-08.thinking.2: Decide the range where intuition from experience applies
y-m-19-08.prereq.0: Sign rules for multiplying and dividing integers
y-m-19-08.s.s1.prompt: How do you judge Minjae's statement at first?
y-m-19-08.s.s1.hint.0: Put specific numbers in for a and b and calculate a÷b and b÷a separately.
y-m-19-08.s.s1.hint.1: Test separately the case of two positive numbers, the case where a negative number is mixed in, and the case where the two numbers are the same.
y-m-19-08.s.s1.o.a: It seems always right. A property that works for multiplication will work for division too
y-m-19-08.s.s1.r.a: Whether a property that holds for multiplication also holds for division has to be tested separately.
y-m-19-08.s.s1.o.b: It seems right sometimes and wrong sometimes. I need to calculate a few examples
y-m-19-08.s.s1.r.b: This is a first step in testing a claim by calculating examples. The judgment is still left open.
y-m-19-08.s.s1.o.c: It seems always wrong. If you swap the order of division, the value will be different
y-m-19-08.s.s1.r.c: You haven't checked whether swapping the order always changes the value. Testing one example shows whether this statement can be broken.
y-m-19-08.s.s1.o.d: It seems right only when both numbers are positive and wrong when a negative number is mixed in. I need to look at examples
y-m-19-08.s.s1.r.d: You guessed that the sign is the cause. First check with examples of positive numbers like 6÷3 and 3÷6.
y-m-19-08.s.s1.explain: If you calculate examples, 6÷3=2 and 3÷6=1/2, so it is not always right. But there are also cases like 3÷3 where they are the same, so it is not 'always wrong' either. Let's go on to find under what condition it is right.
y-m-19-08.s.s2.prompt: Make two pairs (a, b) for which the values of a÷b and b÷a are different. a and b are nonzero integers with absolute value 20 or less. (Count (a, b) and (b, a) as the same example.)
y-m-19-08.s.s2.hint.0: Try two numbers with different absolute values. We will look at what happens when the absolute values are the same next.
y-m-19-08.s.s2.hint.1: If you write division as a fraction, a÷b is a/b and b÷a is b/a. Think about what must be the same for these two to be equal.
y-m-19-08.s.s2.ok.c1: It is a nonzero integer with absolute value 20 or less.
y-m-19-08.s.s2.fail.c1: a and b must be nonzero integers with absolute value 20 or less.
y-m-19-08.s.s2.ok.c2: The values of a÷b and b÷a are different.
y-m-19-08.s.s2.fail.c2: The values of a÷b and b÷a are the same. To be a counterexample, the two values must be different.
y-m-19-08.s.s2.explain: 6÷3=2 but 3÷6=1/2, and 2÷(−8)=−1/4 but (−8)÷2=−4. If even one pair has different values, the claim 'they are always the same' is broken.
y-m-19-08.s.s3.prompt: Still, there are cases where the values of a÷b and b÷a are equal. Give two examples of such (a, b), and say under what condition they are equal.
y-m-19-08.s.s3.hint.0: Write a÷b and b÷a as the fractions a/b and b/a, and think about what relationship the numerator and denominator must have for the two to be equal.
y-m-19-08.s.s3.hint.1: Choose two numbers with the same absolute value and calculate the case where the signs are the same and the case where they are different separately.
y-m-19-08.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you actually calculate a÷b and b÷a for your two examples and check that they are equal?
y-m-19-08.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Are your examples of different kinds, such as one with a=b and the other with a=−b?
y-m-19-08.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you state the condition in words, such as 'the absolute values are the same'?
y-m-19-08.s.s3.model.0: 3÷3 = 1 and 3÷3 is also 1, so they are the same. 3÷(−3) = −1 and (−3)÷3 = −1, so they are the same. They are equal when the absolute values of the two numbers are the same.
y-m-19-08.s.s3.model.1: If a and b are the same number, both are 1, and if they are opposites like 5 and −5, both are −1. That is, the cases where the sizes are the same and only the signs are the same or opposite.
y-m-19-08.s.s3.modelNote.1: A summary of the two kinds of examples as a condition

y-m-19-09.title: If the values are equal at x=2, are they the same expression?
y-m-19-09.topic: Checking whether linear expressions are the same
y-m-19-09.goal: Use a counterexample to confirm that two expressions cannot be called the same just because their values are equal at one value, and tell apart how to show expressions are the same from how to show they are different.
y-m-19-09.material: 'Two expressions are the same' means that the values of the two expressions are always equal no matter what number you put in for the variable. First pick out which of the four pairs below are the same expressions. (3(x−2) is read 'three times the quantity x minus two'.)
y-m-19-09.thinking.0: Decide whether expressions are the same
y-m-19-09.thinking.1: Make a counterexample where only one value is equal
y-m-19-09.prereq.0: Finding the value of an expression by substituting a number for a variable
y-m-19-09.prereq.1: Adding and subtracting linear expressions and removing parentheses
y-m-19-09.s.s1.prompt: Choose all the pairs among the following four whose two expressions always have equal values no matter what number you put in for x.
y-m-19-09.s.s1.hint.0: In each pair, put 0 and 1 in for x and compare the values of the two expressions.
y-m-19-09.s.s1.hint.1: For a pair whose values are different, one try is enough to know the expressions are different. For a pair whose values came out the same, put in more numbers or remove the parentheses to check.
y-m-19-09.s.s1.r.a: Removing the parentheses gives 3x−6+5, and collecting the constants gives 3x−1. The two expressions match.
y-m-19-09.s.s1.r.b: Multiplying 2 by every term inside the parentheses gives 2x+2, and the sum is 3x+2. They differ in one place, the constant term.
y-m-19-09.s.s1.r.c: Multiplying −2 by both x and −3 gives −2x+6, so 4x−2x+6 = 2x+6. The two expressions match.
y-m-19-09.s.s1.r.d: The − in front of the parentheses applies to both terms inside. It gives −x+4, so the sum is x+4, and the sign of the constant term differs from x−4.
y-m-19-09.s.s1.explain: For a and c, removing the parentheses gives the same expression. For b, 2x+2+x = 3x+2, and for d, −x+4+2x = x+4, so the constant terms differ and they are not the same expressions.
y-m-19-09.s.s2.prompt: There is an expression A = 3x+2. When x=2, the value of A is 8. Make three different linear expressions B = px+q that have the same value 8 at x=2 but are not the same expression as A. (p and q are integers from −10 to 10)
y-m-19-09.s.s2.hint.0: First choose a p, and then adjust q so that putting in x=2 gives 8.
y-m-19-09.s.s2.hint.1: Also check what happens if you make p equal to 3.
y-m-19-09.s.s2.ok.c1: p and q are integers from −10 to 10.
y-m-19-09.s.s2.fail.c1: Write p and q as integers from −10 to 10.
y-m-19-09.s.s2.ok.c2: The value of B at x=2 is 8.
y-m-19-09.s.s2.fail.c2: The value of B when you put in x=2 is not 8. Calculate 2×p+q.
y-m-19-09.s.s2.ok.c3: The coefficient differs from A's, so it is not the same expression.
y-m-19-09.s.s2.fail.c3: If p=3, then q=2 and it is the same expression as A. Make it a different expression.
y-m-19-09.s.s2.explain: Expressions whose value is 8 at x=2 include B = x+6, 2x+4, 4x+0, 5x−2. All of them equal A only at x=2; for example, at x=0, A is 2 and B = x+6 is 6.
y-m-19-09.s.s3.prompt: Because the values of the two expressions were equal when you put in x=2, can you say the two expressions are the same expression? If you can't, write the reason, and also write what you would do to show that the two expressions are different.
y-m-19-09.s.s3.hint.0: First pick one of the expressions you made in the previous step and compare its values at x=2 and x=0.
y-m-19-09.s.s3.hint.1: Think about how many values you would need in order to say 'they are the same expression'.
y-m-19-09.s.s3.placeholder: Example: They were equal only at one value, so ...
y-m-19-09.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you separate, in your own words, 'the values are equal' from 'they are the same expression'?
y-m-19-09.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you include that to show they are different expressions, you only need to find one case where the values differ?
y-m-19-09.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you also think about what you should do to show that they are the same expression?

y-m-19-10.title: When the answer to an equation is 13.125, what should we doubt?
y-m-19-10.topic: Checking whether the solution of a linear equation fits the situation
y-m-19-10.goal: Check whether the solution from solving an equation fits the situation of the problem (a count of whole items), and when it does not, decide whether to check the solving, the conditions, or the situation.
y-m-19-10.material: At a stationery store, one pen costs 800원 and one pencil case costs 1500원. Seoa bought x pens and 1 pencil case, paid 12000원, and received no change. Pens are sold only one at a time, and x is the number of pens bought.
y-m-19-10.thinking.0: Estimate first and then check by calculation
y-m-19-10.thinking.1: Decide whether the solution fits the conditions of the situation
y-m-19-10.thinking.2: Change the conditions to make a problem that works
y-m-19-10.prereq.0: Setting up and solving a linear equation
y-m-19-10.prereq.1: Telling natural numbers and decimals apart
y-m-19-10.s.s1.prompt: The information is revealed one piece at a time. Each time, pick what seems most likely to you right now, then check your thinking against the information that follows.
y-m-19-10.s.s1.hint.0: For each piece of information, mark which part of the expression (price, number, amount paid) was newly decided.
y-m-19-10.s.s1.hint.1: Put the answer you chose into the expression and check whether 800×(number of pens)+1500 equals the actual amount.
y-m-19-10.s.s1.st.0.info: What Seoa bought: x pens (800원 each) and 1 pencil case (1500원). Money paid: 12000원. Change: none.
y-m-19-10.s.s1.st.0.ask: Before solving the equation, what do you think about this story?
y-m-19-10.s.s1.st.0.after: Deciding to check after solving is reasonable, and so is estimating that it is about 13 pens and deciding to check by calculation.
y-m-19-10.s.s1.st.0.o.a: I only know after solving. x has to be a natural number to be used as a number of pens
y-m-19-10.s.s1.st.0.r.a: This is the judgment of finding the solution and then checking whether that value fits the condition of the situation (the number of pens).
y-m-19-10.s.s1.st.0.o.b: It is given as a problem, so solving it will surely give a natural number x
y-m-19-10.s.s1.st.0.r.b: Just because it is given as a problem does not guarantee that the answer fits the situation.
y-m-19-10.s.s1.st.0.o.c: It's impossible. 12000 is not divisible by 800
y-m-19-10.s.s1.st.0.r.c: 12000÷800=15, so it is divisible. Also, you need to subtract the pencil case price of 1500원 before thinking about it.
y-m-19-10.s.s1.st.0.o.d: 800×13+1500 is close to 12000, so I estimate about 13 pens and then calculate
y-m-19-10.s.s1.st.0.r.d: You used the order of estimating to make a prediction and checking by calculation. An estimate does not guarantee an exact answer.
y-m-19-10.s.s1.st.1.ask: How do you interpret this result?
y-m-19-10.s.s1.st.1.after: Rechecking the solving first, or believing the solving is right and doubting the conditions, are both reasonable. Using the decimal solution as it is, or rounding it, does not fit the situation.
y-m-19-10.s.s1.st.1.o.a: Accept that Seoa bought 13.125 pens and skip over the change issue
y-m-19-10.s.s1.st.1.r.a: It said pens are sold only one at a time. If the number of pens is a decimal, it does not fit the situation.
y-m-19-10.s.s1.st.1.o.b: If the solving is right, then something in the conditions of this story (price, amount, change) is wrong
y-m-19-10.s.s1.st.1.r.b: The equation was solved, but you doubted the conditions of the problem based on the fact that the solution cannot be used in the situation.
y-m-19-10.s.s1.st.1.o.c: First recheck setting up the equation and the calculation. If it is still right, doubt the conditions
y-m-19-10.s.s1.st.1.r.c: This is the order of checking the solving process first when an answer looks odd. If it is not a mistake, move on to a problem with the conditions.
y-m-19-10.s.s1.st.1.o.d: Round to the first decimal place and answer 14 pens
y-m-19-10.s.s1.st.2.info: New information: The clerk said, "That day Seoa paid 12000원 and got 100원 back in change." (The receipt has not been checked yet.)
y-m-19-10.s.s1.st.2.ask: How does your judgment change with this new information?
y-m-19-10.s.s1.st.2.after: Fixing the conditions with the new information and checking whether x=13 comes out is reasonable, and so is putting off a decision because what the clerk said has not yet been confirmed.
y-m-19-10.s.s1.st.2.o.a: It's explained by x=13. If the amount paid is 11900원, then 800×13+1500 is right
y-m-19-10.s.s1.st.2.r.a: You put the new information into the expression and checked whether the value becomes a natural number.
y-m-19-10.s.s1.st.2.o.b: The story still doesn't work. I think 100원 doesn't change anything
y-m-19-10.s.s1.st.2.r.b: If the actual amount paid is 11900원 instead of 12000원, the expression changes. You did not put the new information into the expression.
y-m-19-10.s.s1.st.2.o.c: The clerk's word alone is not enough. I won't decide until I check the amount paid with the receipt
y-m-19-10.s.s1.st.2.r.c: This is the judgment of considering the source of the information and putting off the decision. Leaving the conclusion open until the basis is confirmed is also reasonable.
y-m-19-10.s.s1.st.2.o.d: 13.125 pens is right, and change has nothing to do with the equation
y-m-19-10.s.s1.st.2.r.d: Change affects the amount paid, so the value on the right side of the expression changes. You can't say it is unrelated.
y-m-19-10.s.s1.reflect: At first, it was before solving, so you left your judgment open, and when the solution became 13.125, the question was whether to doubt the 'solving' or the 'conditions'. The last piece of information changed the value on the right side of the expression. Checking whether the solution fits the situation is a separate check done after the solving is finished.
y-m-19-10.s.s2.prompt: Suppose the prices of a pen and a pencil case stay the same (800원, 1500원), and only the total amount Seoa paid, T (원), changes. Make three different cases in which she bought x pens and 1 pencil case and paid exactly T원 with no change. (T is from 10000원 to 14000원)
y-m-19-10.s.s2.hint.0: Fix x as 11, 12, 13 and calculate 800×x+1500 to find T.
y-m-19-10.s.s2.hint.1: Check that the T you calculated is from 10000 to 14000, and also see whether there is an x that gives 12000원.
y-m-19-10.s.s2.fail.c1: Write the number of pens x as a natural number.
y-m-19-10.s.s2.fail.c2: The value of 800×x+1500 differs from T.
y-m-19-10.s.s2.explain: T = 800x + 1500, so for x=11, 12, 13, 14, 15, T is 10300, 11100, 11900, 12700, 13500. 12000원 is not on this list. The total must be 1500 plus a multiple of 800.

y-m-19-11.title: Is it already decided which of two plans is the better deal?
y-m-19-11.topic: Comparing and using linear expressions (pricing plans)
y-m-19-11.goal: Compare the costs of two plans with expressions in a variable, explain with conditions how the better deal depends on the number of uses, and design a new plan that meets the same criteria.
y-m-19-11.material: A video app has two plans. Plan 가: 1200원 per video, no matter how many videos you watch in a month. Plan 나: pay 6000원 first each month, and each video you watch costs 700원. Let the number of videos watched in a month be x (an integer, 0 or more). The monthly fee for 가 is 1200x원, and the monthly fee for 나 is 6000+700x원.
y-m-19-11.thinking.1: State a judgment that changes depending on the conditions
y-m-19-11.thinking.2: Design a new plan that meets the constraints
y-m-19-11.s.s1.prompt: Minho has not yet decided how many videos to watch in a month. Which plan is a better deal?
y-m-19-11.s.s1.hint.0: Write in a table the fee for each plan when watching 2, 10, and 20 videos in a month, and compare them.
y-m-19-11.s.s1.hint.1: In the table, find near which number of videos the better plan switches.
y-m-19-11.s.s1.o.a: 나 is better. At 700원 per video it is cheaper, so 나 is better no matter how many you watch
y-m-19-11.s.s1.r.a: You compared only the price per video. 나 has the 6000원 paid first, and that share is bigger when you watch few.
y-m-19-11.s.s1.o.b: 가 is better. There is no money paid first, so 가 is better whether you watch few or many
y-m-19-11.s.s1.r.b: You only looked at the advantage of having no money paid first. The more you watch, the more the difference in price per video adds up.
y-m-19-11.s.s1.o.c: Which is better depends on the number watched. The number where the fees become equal is the boundary
y-m-19-11.s.s1.r.c: This is the judgment that the better plan changes around the point where the two fees are equal. You need to find the number of videos that serves as the boundary.
y-m-19-11.s.s1.o.d: The monthly fees of the two plans are the same, so there is no difference whichever you choose
y-m-19-11.s.s1.r.d: The price per video and the money paid first are different, so the values differ depending on the number. You can see this by trying one or two values.
y-m-19-11.s.s1.explain: 가 is 1200x and 나 is 6000+700x, so the number where they are equal is 1200x = 6000+700x, that is, x=12. With fewer than 12 videos 가 is cheaper, and with more, 나 is cheaper.
y-m-19-11.s.s2.prompt: Find three different numbers of videos per month x for which 나 is cheaper than 가. (x is an integer from 0 to 40)
y-m-19-11.s.s2.hint.0: Find both fees when x=12 and compare them. See what happens when you choose a number greater or smaller than that value.
y-m-19-11.s.s2.hint.1: Each time you pick a candidate, calculate the two fees separately and check which one is greater.
y-m-19-11.s.s2.var.x: The number of videos watched in a month x (videos)
y-m-19-11.s.s2.ok.c1: It is an integer from 0 to 40.
y-m-19-11.s.s2.fail.c1: Write x as an integer from 0 to 40.
y-m-19-11.s.s2.ok.c2: The fee for 나 is cheaper than the fee for 가.
y-m-19-11.s.s2.fail.c2: The fee for 나 is not cheaper than the fee for 가. Calculate each of the two fees and compare them.
y-m-19-11.s.s2.explain: For 나 to be cheaper, 6000+700x < 1200x, that is, x > 12. 나 is cheaper from 13 videos on, and at 12 videos both are the same, 14400원.
y-m-19-11.s.s3.prompt: Make a new plan '다'. Plan 다 charges f원 first each month and p원 per video. Conditions: when watching 10 videos in a month, the fee must be equal to 가 (12000원), the money paid first f must be 1000원 or more, and the price per video p must be 100원 or more. (f and p are integers)
y-m-19-11.s.s3.hint.0: First choose a p, and then adjust f so that the fee for 10 videos is 12000.
y-m-19-11.s.s3.hint.1: With the f and p you chose, compare the fees for 5, 10, and 15 videos with 가.
y-m-19-11.s.s3.ok.c1: f is an integer of 1000 or more and p is an integer of 100 or more.
y-m-19-11.s.s3.fail.c1: Write f as an integer of 1000 or more and p as an integer of 100 or more.
y-m-19-11.s.s3.ok.c2: For 10 videos, it is 12000원, the same as 가.
y-m-19-11.s.s3.fail.c2: The fee f+10×p for watching 10 videos is not 12000원.
y-m-19-11.s.s3.explain: If f+10p = 12000, then (f, p) = (2000, 1000), (4000, 800), (6000, 600), (1000, 1100), and so on. If p is less than 1200, 다 is cheaper than 가 when you watch more than 10 videos, and 가 is cheaper when you watch fewer than 10.

y-m-19-12.title: How will '2x+1/3' be read in a chat window?
y-m-19-12.topic: Notation of expressions with variables and parentheses
y-m-19-12.goal: Confirm that parentheses decide the order of calculation in the notation of expressions with variables, and rewrite the expression in the message so the reader will not misunderstand.
y-m-19-12.material: In a chat window you can't write a fraction with a horizontal bar, so / is used to show division. Seoyeon sent a friend this message: "The area is 2x+1/3." In math, multiplication and division are calculated before addition, and 2x is the product of 2 and x. (2x is read 'two x'.)
y-m-19-12.thinking.0: Decide whether the same characters are read as different expressions
y-m-19-12.thinking.1: Check how much the value changes depending on how it is read
y-m-19-12.thinking.2: Rewrite the expression with the reader in mind
y-m-19-12.prereq.0: Notation for multiplication and division in expressions with variables (2x is 2×x, a÷b is a/b)
y-m-19-12.prereq.1: Finding the value of an expression
y-m-19-12.s.s1.prompt: When x=4, what is the value of the expression '2x+1/3' in the message if you calculate it by the rules of math?
y-m-19-12.s.s1.hint.0: In the expression in the message, first find the calculations that are not addition (multiplication, division) and mark them.
y-m-19-12.s.s1.hint.1: Do the marked calculations, and then do the remaining addition last.
y-m-19-12.s.s1.r.a: You calculated 2x=8 first and then added 1/3. Multiplication and division come before addition.
y-m-19-12.s.s1.r.b: There are no parentheses, yet you added x and 1 first. 2x is calculated first as 2×4.
y-m-19-12.s.s1.r.c: You did the addition first and then divided by 3. The division attaches only to the 1/3 part.
y-m-19-12.s.s1.o.d: Each person who receives it may read it differently, so the value can't be decided as one
y-m-19-12.s.s1.r.d: The worry that someone who doesn't know the rules may read it differently is fair. Still, if you apply the rules, the value is decided.
y-m-19-12.s.s1.explain: 2x is 2×4=8, and 1/3 is division so it is calculated before addition. 8 + 1/3 = 25/3.
y-m-19-12.s.s1.acc.0: By the rules it is decided to be 25/3, but the worry that some readers may remember the rules differently is reasonable. In the next step, think about how to reduce this worry.
y-m-19-12.s.s2.prompt: There are two ways of reading it. (가) Reading by the rules: the value of 2x plus 1/3. (나) Misreading: the value of (2x+1) divided by 3. When you put a natural number from 1 to 12 in for x, find three different x for which the difference between the values of the two readings is 7 or more.
y-m-19-12.s.s2.hint.0: Pick a few, like x=2, 6, calculate the values of (가) and (나) for each, and write them in a table.
y-m-19-12.s.s2.hint.1: In the table, look at how the difference between the two values changes as x gets bigger.
y-m-19-12.s.s2.ok.c1: It is a natural number from 1 to 12.
y-m-19-12.s.s2.fail.c1: Write x as a natural number from 1 to 12.
y-m-19-12.s.s2.ok.c2: The difference between the values of the two readings is 7 or more.
y-m-19-12.s.s2.fail.c2: The difference between the values of the two readings is less than 7. Calculate the two values and find the difference.
y-m-19-12.s.s2.explain: (가)−(나) = (2x+1/3) − (2x+1)/3 = 4x/3, so for the difference to be 7 or more, x must be 6 or more. If x=6, (가) is 12 and 1/3 and (나) is 4 and 1/3, so the difference is 8. The bigger x gets, the bigger the difference.
y-m-19-12.s.s3.prompt: If Seoyeon wants to say the value of (2x+1) divided by 3, how should it be written on one line using only keyboard characters in the chat window so there is no misunderstanding? Write the expression and explain in one sentence why you wrote it that way.
y-m-19-12.s.s3.hint.0: First decide whether what is divided by 3 is only 2x or the whole of 2x+1.
y-m-19-12.s.s3.hint.1: Put x=4 into the expression you wrote and check whether the calculated value is the one you want (3).
y-m-19-12.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you check by putting numbers in for x that the expression you wrote, read by the rules, gives the value of (2x+1) divided by 3?
y-m-19-12.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you imagine how your friend would read it and reduce the places for misunderstanding?
y-m-19-12.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you also think of ways to make it easier to read, such as using a multiplication sign (*)?
y-m-19-12.s.s3.model.0: I'll write (2x+1)/3. Putting 2x+1 in parentheses makes it clear that all of it is divided by 3 at once, so no one reads it differently.
y-m-19-12.s.s3.model.1: Write it like (2*x+1)/3 and put in parentheses so the order of calculation isn't misunderstood. Also use the multiplication sign * to make clear that 2 and x are separate.
y-m-19-12.s.s3.modelNote.1: A safe notation that even includes the multiplication sign

y-m-19-13.title: Can you catch up with a friend who left earlier in front of the school?
y-m-19-13.goal: Compare the result of finding, with an equation, the time and place where two people with different speeds meet to the limit on the length of the road (the distance to the school), decide, and correct your judgment with new information.
y-m-19-13.material: A and B start from the same place and walk to school along the same straight road in the same direction. The distance to the school will be told later. A starts first and walks at 4 km/h, and B walks at 6 km/h starting 30 minutes (0.5 hours) after A starts. While they are walking, each one's speed is constant.
y-m-19-13.thinking.0: Compare the value from the equation with the conditions of the situation
y-m-19-13.thinking.1: Decide whether new information changes the conclusion
y-m-19-13.thinking.2: Find the wrong line in a solution
y-m-19-13.prereq.1: Setting up and solving a linear equation
y-m-19-13.s.s1.prompt: The information is revealed one piece at a time. Each time, pick what seems most likely to you right now, then check your thinking against the information that follows.
y-m-19-13.s.s1.hint.0: For each piece of information, mark whether what was newly decided is the time, the place, or the speed.
y-m-19-13.s.s1.hint.1: For the answer you chose, write in numbers where the two people are at that moment and compare.
y-m-19-13.s.s1.st.0.info: A walks at 4 km/h and B walks at 6 km/h. B starts 30 minutes later than A. The distance to the school has not been told yet.
y-m-19-13.s.s1.st.0.ask: Can B catch up with A?
y-m-19-13.s.s1.st.0.after: Judging that B catches up if the road is long enough is reasonable, and so is deciding to calculate the distance A went ahead and the speed at which B closes in.
y-m-19-13.s.s1.st.0.o.a: If the road is long enough, B catches up. The gap shrinks because of the difference in speed per hour
y-m-19-13.s.s1.st.0.r.a: You saw that a faster speed can make up the distance A went ahead as time passes.
y-m-19-13.s.s1.st.0.o.b: B can't catch up. B started 30 minutes late, so it can't make up the distance
y-m-19-13.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You did not think about how the difference in speed builds up as time passes.
y-m-19-13.s.s1.st.0.o.c: I need to calculate to know. Compare the distance A went ahead with the distance B closes
y-m-19-13.s.s1.st.0.r.c: This is a method of deciding the time and place by comparing the distance went ahead with the speed of closing in.
y-m-19-13.s.s1.st.0.o.d: B will surely catch up no matter how long the road is. B is faster, so the length doesn't matter
y-m-19-13.s.s1.st.0.r.d: If the road has a limited length, it may end before they meet.
y-m-19-13.s.s1.st.1.info: Suppose they meet t hours after B starts. Then the distance B walked, 6t (km), equals the distance A walked, 4(t+0.5) (km). From 6t = 4(t+0.5), t = 1 hour, and the meeting place is 6km from the starting point. The school is 5km from the starting point, and the road ends at the school.
y-m-19-13.s.s1.st.1.ask: Will B catch up with A before arriving at the school?
y-m-19-13.s.s1.st.1.after: Comparing the meeting place (6km) with the end of the road (5km) is reasonable, and so is deciding to directly compare the arrival times. A reaches the school 75 minutes after starting, and B reaches it 50 minutes after B starts (80 minutes after A starts), so A arrives first.
y-m-19-13.s.s1.st.1.o.a: B catches up. 6km and 5km are not much different, so they almost meet in front of the school
y-m-19-13.s.s1.st.1.r.a: If the meeting place is beyond the school, they can't meet in front of the school. Before judging that it is 'about the same', you must compare which one reaches the school first.
y-m-19-13.s.s1.st.1.o.b: B can't catch up. The meeting place (6km) is farther than the school (5km), so A arrives first
y-m-19-13.s.s1.st.1.r.b: You decided by comparing the place you found with the end of the road. That is checking whether the solution of the equation is within the range of the situation.
y-m-19-13.s.s1.st.1.o.c: Directly compare the times when the two people arrive at the school
y-m-19-13.s.s1.st.1.r.c: This is another way to check, using the arrival time instead of the meeting place. You can see whether the same conclusion comes out.
y-m-19-13.s.s1.st.1.o.d: B catches up. B is faster, so B also arrives at the school first
y-m-19-13.s.s1.st.1.r.d: You did not compare the time B reaches the school with the time A reaches it. A has in effect already left from 4km ahead.
y-m-19-13.s.s1.st.2.info: New information: 15 minutes after A started, at the 1km point, A stopped to tie a shoelace and rested for 10 minutes, then walked again at 4 km/h (A does not walk during the rest). B's start time and speed stay the same.
y-m-19-13.s.s1.st.2.ask: How does your judgment change with this new information?
y-m-19-13.s.s1.st.2.after: Whether you put the time A rested into the equation and find that the meeting place is the 4km point (4(t+0.5−1/6)=6t, t=2/3 hours), or judge that the order of arrival times changed, the conclusion is the same. You corrected your earlier judgment with the new information.
y-m-19-13.s.s1.st.2.o.a: B catches up. They meet near the 4km point, so it is before reaching the school (5km)
y-m-19-13.s.s1.st.2.r.a: You judged that the meeting place moved up to before the school by putting the time A rested into the equation.
y-m-19-13.s.s1.st.2.o.b: B can't catch up. Even with the rest, the conclusion that A arrives at the school first stays the same
y-m-19-13.s.s1.st.2.r.b: A's arrival time gets later by the length of the rest. You have to reflect the new information and compare the arrival times again.
y-m-19-13.s.s1.st.2.o.c: Can't tell. I need to know more about where and when A rested to decide whether B catches up
y-m-19-13.s.s1.st.2.r.c: The place of the rest (1km) and the time (10 minutes starting 15 minutes after A's start) are already given, and it ended before B started.
y-m-19-13.s.s1.st.2.o.d: Compare the arrival times. B arrives at 80 minutes and A at 85 minutes, so B arrives first
y-m-19-13.s.s1.st.2.r.d: You confirmed the same conclusion with another method. If the order of arrival times is reversed, it means they passed each other on the way.
y-m-19-13.s.s1.reflect: With the second piece of information, your judgment changed by comparing the solution of the equation (6km) with the limit of the length (5km), and with the third piece, the conditions changed so the answer to the same question changed. Look back at how the habit of checking whether the value you found actually happens in the situation changed your judgment.
y-m-19-13.s.s2.prompt: This is Seoha's solution for the time B catches up with A (the first situation, with no rest). Choose the first line that is wrong.
y-m-19-13.s.s2.hint.0: Put t=0.25 into the distances B and A walked and calculate whether they are equal.
y-m-19-13.s.s2.hint.1: For each line, write what quantity the expression represents, with units (hours, km), and check whether it is right.
y-m-19-13.s.s2.line.0: Suppose they meet t hours after B starts.
y-m-19-13.s.s2.line.1: The distance B walked at that time is 6t km.
y-m-19-13.s.s2.line.2: A started 30 minutes earlier, so the time A walked is (t+0.5) hours, and the distance walked is 4t+0.5 km.
y-m-19-13.s.s2.explain: Line 3 is wrong. The time A walked is (t+0.5) hours, so the distance walked is 4×(t+0.5) = 4t+2 km. You must multiply the speed 4 by the 0.5 hours too. This error carried on through lines 4 and 5 and gave t=0.25. Checking the answer: when t=0.25, B has walked 1.5km and A has walked 4×0.75=3km, which differ.
